title: Nobody Taught Me How to Sell
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: The Art of Asking Questions (andreachiarelli.substack.com), May 16, 2026
summary: Andrea Chiarelli opens with a vivid personal scene: sent to a professional services conference as a junior with a vague brief to 'represent the firm,' arriving without any mental model of what success looked like, and leaving with a pocket full of business cards and a nagging sense of having missed the point. From this vignette, she develops a structural argument about how professional services firms systematically fail junior colleagues in business development: the expectation is universal, its definition is absent, and the gap is treated as a performance problem (lack of initiative) rather than a learning and development problem (lack of clarity and support). She reframes what BD actually looks like at junior level—not pitching or closing but embedded relational behaviors: noticing client needs in passing, asking follow-up questions, spotting patterns across conversations, making connections between client problems and team expertise. Five design approaches are proposed: making the invisible visible (leaders narrating their thinking, not just their actions), starting small and specific (observable micro-behaviors rather than abstract expectations), learning through real work, framing BD as a team activity, and building in reflection and feedback. The article is grounded in adult learning theory (adults engage more readily when learning is clearly relevant and actionable) and concludes that capability in business development accumulates through a long series of small, specific, well-supported attempts—not through osmosis or pressure.
points: Junior professionals receive universally vague BD expectations ('contribute to business development') without any translation of what that means at their career stage; the same instruction is given to analysts and senior managers though the implied behaviors are entirely different.

Business development for juniors is not pitching or closing—it is embedded relational attention: noticing client needs in passing, asking deepening questions, spotting patterns across conversations, making connections between client problems and team expertise.

Reframing vague BD expectations from a performance problem to a learning and development problem changes the response: performance framing produces pressure and firmer expectations; L&D; framing produces design—small, deliberate choices about how people are introduced to the work.

Capability in business development accumulates through a long series of small, specific, well-supported attempts; firms that design those attempts produce consultants with real instincts; firms that don't produce senior consultants still occasionally uncertain in conference rooms.

Experience without reflection doesn't create learning; ten minutes of structured debrief—asking specifically what was noticed and what would be tried next time—converts raw experience into developmental capital.
quotes: I knew, without anyone having said so directly, that I was meant to be doing something that looked like selling. That was presumably the reason I'd been sent. But I'd never sold anything in my life. Up to that point my career had been about delivering: running analyses, drafting decks, sitting in client meetings and taking careful notes.

For most junior colleagues, the actual contribution has very little to do with pitching or closing deals. It tends to show up in smaller, more embedded ways: Noticing a client need in passing that could lead to follow-on work. Asking a follow-up question in a meeting that deepens understanding of a problem.

The reframe from lack of initiative to lack of clarity and support is important because it changes what the problem actually is: treated as a performance issue, the response tends to be firmer expectations or more pressure, neither of which reliably changes behaviour. Treated as a learning and development challenge, the response becomes design.

Vague expectations create hesitation; concrete actions create entry points. 'Get involved in business development' is a task that's hard to start. 'Listen for one thing the client mentions twice in this meeting' is a task you can start immediately.

Capability in business development accumulates slowly, through a long series of small, specific, well-supported attempts. The firms that invest in designing those attempts tend to produce junior consultants who, a few years in, have developed real instincts for this work.
Whether they come away from it having learned something, or simply having survived it, depends a great deal on how the firm around them has chosen to design the experience.
